questions.stem: Explain how a transit planner would turn the mass of a uniform cylindrical component into a formula that can be used for any radius and length.

answer.exemplar: Uniform density means the mass is the density multiplied by the volume, and the volume of a solid cylinder is the area of its circular base times its length, so m = ρπr²h. questions.topic: Volume of a ball in spherical coordinates
questions.learningObjective: Set up and evaluate the spherical integral for a ball.
questions.stem: Describe the setup and evaluation that gives the volume of a ball of radius R using spherical coordinates with the volume element dV = ρ² sin θ dρ dθ dφ.

answer.exemplar: A ball centred at the origin is described by 0 ≤ ρ ≤ R, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, and 0 ≤ φ ≤ 2π. Multiplying the element ρ² sin θ dρ dθ dφ over these bounds gives ∫₀^R ρ² dρ · ∫₀^π sin θ dθ · ∫₀^{2π} dφ = (R³/3)(2)(2π) = 4πR³/3, which is the standard ball volume.

questions.explanation: The ball is 0 ≤ ρ ≤ R, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π, 0 ≤ φ ≤ 2π, and the integral splits into (R³/3)(2)(2π) = 4πR³/3. Restricting θ to a half-range, or dropping it, loses half the solid.
questions.hint: The polar range must cover the whole sphere, 0 to pi.

questions.topic: Volume of a spherical shell
questions.learningObjective: Explain why shell volume is the difference of two ball volumes.
questions.stem: Explain why the volume of a spherical shell is found by subtracting two ball volumes, and give the resulting formula for inner radius a and outer radius b.

answer.exemplar: A shell is the set of points whose distance from the centre lies between a and b, so it is precisely the outer ball of radius b with the inner ball of radius a removed. Because volume is additive, the shell's volume is (4/3)πb³ − (4/3)πa³ = (4/3)π(b³ − a³). The cubes must be taken separately, since (b − a)³ is the volume of a ball whose radius is the thickness, not the volume of the shell.

questions.explanation: Removing the inner ball from the outer one leaves the shell exactly, and the volumes subtract to give (4/3)π(b³ − a³). The cubes come first, since (b − a)³ scales like the thickness, not the shell.
questions.hint: Cube each radius first, then subtract them.

questions.stem: Explain how the polar angle θ of a point with spherical coordinates (ρ, θ, φ) relates to its Cartesian height z, and how a planner would compute it from a known radius and height.

answer.exemplar: The z-coordinate of a point in spherical coordinates is z = ρ cos θ, because the polar angle is measured from the positive z-axis and ρ is the distance from the origin. Solving for the angle gives cos θ = z/ρ, so θ = arccos(z/ρ), which is defined for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π. A planner with a measured radius and height therefore takes the arccosine of the height divided by the radius, and the azimuthal angle φ has no effect on this computation.

questions.explanation: Measuring from the z-axis gives z = ρ cos θ, hence θ = arccos(z/ρ). Putting the horizontal offset into that ratio, or measuring from the horizontal plane, returns the complementary angle.
questions.hint: Height equals radius times cosine of the polar angle.

answer.exemplar: The volume of water is the integral of the surface height over the circular cross-section of the tank. questions.learningObjective: Diagnose a mass calculation that dropped one factor of the formula.
questions.stem: A colleague computes the mass of a solid cylinder with radius 0.2 m, length 5 m, and density 2000 kg/m³ as 80π kg, using πr²hρ. What is the likely error?

options.text: The density was written as 200 instead of 2000 kg/m³.
options.misconception: blames a density slip when the length was left out

options.text: The length of 5 m was left out, so the volume became the base area πr².
The radius was doubled to 0.4 m, quadrupling the base area instead of halving it.
options.misconception: claims a doubled radius would reduce the mass

options.text: The factor 2π for a full cylinder was applied on top of πr²h.
options.misconception: believes the cylinder formula has an extra factor of two

questions.explanation: The correct mass is 2000·π(0.2)²(5) = 400π ≈ 1256.6 kg; the reported 80π is one fifth of that, exactly what dropping the 5 m length produces.
questions.hint: Check which factor of the formula was skipped.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Volume of a half ball
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a half ball volume follows from the spherical integral.
questions.stem: Explain how to obtain the volume of a half ball from the spherical integral, and state the resulting expression in terms of the radius.

answer.exemplar: A half ball taken above the equatorial plane is described by 0 ≤ ρ ≤ R, 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, and 0 ≤ φ ≤ 2π, using the element ρ² sin θ dρ dθ dφ. Integrating gives (R³/3)(1)(2π) = 2πR³/3, which is exactly half of the full ball volume 4πR³/3 because the polar range has been halved from π to π/2.

questions.explanation: Halving the polar range from π to π/2 halves the integral to 2πR³/3, matching half the sphere's volume. If the sine factor or the ρ² factor is missing, the halved range no longer fits.
questions.hint: Halve the polar range, keep the element intact.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Polar angle of a point in spherical coordinates
questions.learningObjective: Find the polar angle and the radius of a point in two stages.
questions.stem: A planner's survey marks a point 3 m above the station origin and 4 m horizontally from it. Stage 1: identify the polar angle of that point. Stage 2: which option states the angle and the radius of the point?

options.text: The polar angle is 0.6435 radians and the radius of the point is 5 metres.
The polar angle is 0.9273 radians and the radius of the point is 5 metres.
options.misconception: measures the angle from the horizontal instead of the z-axis

options.text: The polar angle is 0.6435 radians and the radius of the point is 7 metres.
options.misconception: adds the height and the offset instead of the hypotenuse

options.text: The polar angle is 0.9273 radians and the radius of the point is 7 metres.
options.misconception: adds the legs and measures from the wrong reference line

questions.explanation: The point is 3 m up and 4 m across, so its distance from the origin is 5 m and cos θ = 3/5, giving θ = 0.6435 rad. The 0.9273 rad figure is measured from the horizontal plane.
questions.hint: Take the hypotenuse first, then the cosine of the angle.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Volume inside a cylinder below a tilted plane
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a tilt does not change the volume over a symmetric disk.
questions.stem: A planner's cylindrical tank has a water surface given by the plane z = 3 + 0.5x. Why does the tilt not change the volume of water compared with a level surface at z = 3?

options.text: The disk is symmetric, so the 0.5x term integrates to zero over the cross-section.
The tilt only moves water from one side to the other, so the total is unchanged.
options.misconception: believes a tilt can never change any measurement

options.text: The plane has the same average height, so the volumes must coincide for any shape.
options.misconception: assumes equal average height always means equal volume

options.text: The volume depends only on the disk's area, which the tilt leaves unchanged.
options.misconception: believes the disk area alone fixes the volume

questions.explanation: The volume integrates the height over the disk, and the tilted part 0.5x is odd while the disk is symmetric, so it cancels and the volume is 3πr².
questions.hint: Odd terms vanish over a symmetric region.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Volume of a cone in spherical coordinates
questions.learningObjective: Compute the volume of a cone in cubic metres.
questions.stem: A planner's depot roof is a cone of base radius 5 m and height 12 m. What is the volume of that cone in cubic metres, rounded to two decimals?
questions.explanation: The cone's volume is (1/3)π(5²)(12) = 100π ≈ 314.16 m³. Taking the full cylinder gives 942.48 m³, and using the slant height of 13 m mixes up two different lengths.
questions.hint: Cone volume is a third of the cylinder with the same base.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Polar angle of a point in spherical coordinates
questions.learningObjective: Match the bounds of a spherical integral to the differentials.
questions.stem: A planner's spherical tank drawing marks the centre of a ball of radius 6 m with the vertical axis through the centre. Which pairing of bounds and differentials describes the ball?

options.text: ∫₀^6∫₀^{2π}∫₀^π ρ² sin θ dρ dθ dφ, where each bound is paired with the next integral.
options.misconception: believes the written order of the integrals fixes it

options.text: ∫₀^6∫₀^{π/2}∫₀^{2π} ρ² sin θ dρ dθ dφ, which also evaluates to 288π m³.
options.misconception: halves the polar range yet keeps the full sphere value

options.text: ∫₀^6∫₀^π∫₀^{2π} ρ² dρ dθ dφ, since the polar factor cancels over the range.
options.misconception: halves the polar range yet keeps the full value

options.text: ∫₀^6∫₀^π∫₀^{2π} ρ² sin θ dρ dθ dφ, which evaluates to 288π m³.

questions.explanation: A ball of radius 6 needs ρ from 0 to 6, θ over 0 to π, and φ over 0 to 2π, giving (216/3)(2)(2π) = 288π ≈ 904.78 m³. Mismatched bounds describe another region.
questions.hint: Pair each bound with the right differential and angle.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Volume of a spherical shell
questions.learningObjective: Compute the volume of spherical shell material in cubic metres.
questions.stem: A planner sizes a protective shell with inner radius 1.5 m and outer radius 2.5 m. What is the shell volume in cubic metres, rounded to two decimals?
questions.explanation: Subtract the inner ball from the outer one: (4/3)π(2.5³ − 1.5³) = (4/3)π(12.25) = 16.3333π ≈ 51.31 m³. Cubing the radius difference, or adding the two volumes, describes a different solid.
questions.hint: Difference of cubes, then the ball formula.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Volume of a cone in spherical coordinates
questions.learningObjective: Set up a cone in spherical coordinates and evaluate its volume.
questions.stem: A planner models a mast's mast's conical cover with its apex at the origin, a half-angle α, and a flat base at height 5 m whose rim lies 4 m from the axis. Stage 1: write the spherical description of the region. Stage 2: which option states it and the volume of the cone?

options.text: 0 ≤ θ ≤ α with tan α = 4/5 and 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 5, with a volume of 20π m³.
options.misconception: caps the radius at the base height instead of the base plane

options.text: 0 ≤ θ ≤ α with tan α = 4/5 and 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 5 sec θ, with a volume of 80π m³.
options.misconception: forgets the one-third factor of the cone formula

options.text: 0 ≤ θ ≤ α with tan α = 4/5 and 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 5 sec θ, with a volume of 80π/3 ≈ 83.78 m³.
0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2 with 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 5 sec θ and 0 ≤ φ ≤ 2π, with a volume of 80π/3 m³.
options.misconception: fixes the polar range at a right angle for every cone

questions.explanation: The cone is bounded by the half-angle with tan α = 4/5 and the base plane z = 5, and the volume is (1/3)π(4²)(5) = 80π/3 ≈ 83.78 m³. A constant radius cap describes a different region.
questions.hint: A flat base becomes a radial bound, not a fixed radius.
